accuracy.reason: Source audit supports bounded cache behavior, application ownership, independent copies and overload risk; diagrams depict hit/miss and stale copy without automatic synchronization.

evidence.quote: Invalidation alone does not guarantee freshness.

mechanisms.reason: Cards 1-7 identify actors, copy creation, key selection, overlapping old refill, lifetime, copy placement and shared refill; learner transfers those causal steps.

evidence.quote: Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.

coherence.reason: Reuse motivates hit/miss; application ownership and keys precede stale writes, expiry and topology; load risk then informs the final decision. Selective examples clarify keys and the race.

evidence.quote: Include the inputs that change the answer.

decisions.reason: Costs accompany benefits; source validation, shared-cache consequences and capped fallback support decisions. Card 8 explicitly teaches declining low-reuse or freshness-incompatible caches.

evidence.quote: If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.

clarity.reason: Plain actor-led operations define cache-aside, key, invalidation, TTL, eviction and coalescing; the currency and old-price examples explain distinct mechanisms.

evidence.quote: An entry can be evicted before its TTL ends.

outcomes.reason: C1-C5: learner explains reuse and latency/source benefit, station plus language key, hit return, application-owned read/fill/return miss, and remaining database plus cache costs; cards 1-3 teach each step.
C1-C4: learner traces old refill after deletion, rejects freshness guarantee and bypasses cache for source reads; card 4 teaches held old value, deletion timing and authoritative validation.
C1-C4: learner correctly resolves both timelines, lifetime versus freshness/residence, and expiration versus space eviction; cards 2 and 5 teach subsequent application reload.

C1-C5: learner selects shared entry, traces untouched local copies, network versus in-process reads, cost and per-instance versus common loss of cache access; card 6 explicitly teaches these limits without claiming request failure.

C1-C5: learner explains concurrent duplicate reads, one shared lookup, 10000 versus 500 outage overload and bounded fallback with rejection. Optional stale copy is explicitly conditional on accessibility, so no inaccessible-cache assumption; card 7 teaches the required safe path.

C1-C5: learner rejects single-use caching, explains no later reuse, latency/capacity headroom, writes/storage costs and repetition with meaningful source work as reconsideration trigger; cards 1 and 8 support all, including freshness restriction in card 8.

sourceChecks.claim: Live Azure caching guidance confirms reuse benefits, source-work and storage/maintenance costs.
Live Azure cache-aside steps 1-3 confirm API check, source read, cache fill and return; hit/miss diagram is semantically consistent.
Live Azure caching guidance confirms application-maintained copies and unique identifying keys; privacy requires answer-affecting inputs.
Live Azure cache-aside consistency section explicitly denies general consistency; an already fetched old value can refill after deletion, so no cancellation/freshness guarantee follows.
Live Redis eviction page confirms LRU, capacity removal and noeviction; linked Redis EXPIRE confirms timeout deletes a key, not a source refresh.
Live AWS caching article confirms per-process divergent copies, shared service network/operating costs and cache-fleet unavailability; losing one local copy leaves others intact.
Live AWS caching article confirms cold-cache downstream overload, request coalescing and rate-limited fallback; stale fallback requires an accessible copy, and bounded rejection is sufficient here.
Live Azure caching guidance and AWS article confirm reuse/read-cost/freshness considerations and that unique results can make cache overhead unjustified.
